items.readable_text:
Content:
We're used to seeing definite integrals where the limits of integration are constants. For example,

Content:
[MATH: \displaystyle \int_{\color{red}0}^{\color{blue}{2}} t^2\,\textrm d t.]

Content:
Here, the lower limit is [MATH: t={\color{red}{0}}] and the upper limit is [MATH: t={\color{blue}{2}}.]

Content:
What do we get if we allow one of the integration limits to vary? Let's explore this idea by changing the upper integration limit to [MATH: t={\color{blue}{x}}.]

Content:
[MATH: \displaystyle \int_{\color{red}{0}}^{\color{blue}{x}} t^2\,\textrm d t]

Content:
We can evaluate this integral in the usual way:

Content:
[MATH: ∫_{0}^{x}t^{2}dt|= (1)/(3)t^{3}|_{0}^{x}; = (1)/(3)x^{3} − 0; = (1)/(3)x^{3}]

Content:
So, evaluating the integral now gives a function of [MATH: x] instead of a number. This means we can define a new function [MATH: F(x)] as

Content:
[MATH: F(x) = \int_0^x t^2\,\textrm d t.]

Content:
The function [MATH: F(x)] represents the area accumulated by the function [MATH: f(t)=t^2] between [MATH: t=0] and [MATH: t=x.] Different values of [MATH: x] will give different values for the area.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/812c461c1b7ac3a89eafaef2849bb2ce]

Content:
Any function [MATH: F(x)] defined as
[MATH: F(x) = \int_a^x f(t)\,\textrm d t]
is called an accumulation function.

sections.normalized_html: Calculate [MATH: F(\pi)] where [MATH: \displaystyle F(x) = \int_1^x \dfrac 1 t\,\textrm d t.]
sections.readable_text: Calculate [MATH: F(\pi)] where [MATH: \displaystyle F(x) = \int_1^x \dfrac 1 t\,\textrm d t.]

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
Evaluating [MATH: F(x)] at [MATH: x=\pi,] we get the following definite integral: [MATH: F\!\left(\pi\right) = \int_{1}^{\pi} \dfrac{1}{t} \, \textrm{d}t]

Then, computing the definite integral, we get [MATH: F(π)|= ∫_{1}^{π}(1)/(t)dt; = \ln|t||_{1}^{π}; = \ln π − \ln 1; = \ln π.]

sections.normalized_html: The graph of a function [MATH: y = f(x)] is shown below. Given [MATH: \displaystyle g(t)= \int_{-2}^{t} f(x)\, \textrm{d}x,] determine the value of [MATH: g(3).]
sections.readable_text:
The graph of a function [MATH: y = f(x)] is shown below. Given [MATH: \displaystyle g(t)= \int_{-2}^{t} f(x)\, \textrm{d}x,] determine the value of [MATH: g(3).]

[IMG: /graphics/6a389b5bb31f7ee2ea2b8194d93fdc6d]

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
Evaluating [MATH: g(t)] at [MATH: t=3,] we get the following definite integral: [MATH: g(3) = \int_{-2}^{3} f(x)\, \textrm{d}x]

This integral gives the signed area between the curve and the [MATH: x]-axis shown below.

Note that the graph above consists of [MATH: 2] parts:

  • [MATH: x \in [-2,0],] for which the region between the curve and the [MATH: x]-axis is a trapezoid. This corresponds to the area [MATH: A_1.]

  • [MATH: x \in [0,3],] for which the region between the curve and the [MATH: x]-axis is another trapezoid. This corresponds to the area [MATH: A_2.]

Therefore, we can write the integral as follows: [MATH: g(3) = \int_{-2}^{3} f(x) \, \textrm{d}x = \underbrace{\int_{-2}^{0} f(x) \, \textrm{d}x}_{A_1} + \underbrace{\int_{0}^{3} f(x) \, \textrm{d}x}_{A_2}]

Now, let's compute these integrals:

  • To find the first integral where [MATH: x \in [-2,0],] we compute the area [MATH: A_1] of the trapezoid as follows: [MATH: A_{1}|= (1)/(2) ⋅ 2 ⋅ (2 + 3); = 5]

  • To find the second integral where [MATH: x \in [0,3],] we compute the area [MATH: A_2] of the trapezoid as follows: [MATH: A_{2}|= (1)/(2) ⋅ 3 ⋅ (2 + 4); = 9]

Therefore, we obtain [MATH: g(3)|= ∫_{− 2}^{3}f(x)dx = A_{1} + A_{2} = 5 + 9 = 14.]

items.readable_text:
Content:
When we create an accumulation function by integrating a "rate of change" function, the accumulation function describes the "net change" of the system.

Content:
To describe this in more detail, suppose that [MATH: f(t)] is continuous and [MATH: F'(t) = f(t)] for [MATH: t\in [a,b].] From the fundamental theorem of calculus, we know that

Content:
[MATH: F(b) - F(a) = \int_a^b f(t)\,\textrm d t.]

Content:
The equation above can be rewritten as

Content:
[MATH: F(b) = F(a) + \int_a^b f(t)\,\textrm d t.]

Content:
If we let the upper limit vary, so setting [MATH: b=x,] we have

Content:
[MATH: F(x) = F(a) + \int_a^x f(t)\,\textrm d t.]

Content:
This formula tells us that the value of [MATH: F] at an arbitrary point [MATH: x] equals the value of [MATH: F] at some starting point [MATH: a] plus the accumulation of the rate of change of [MATH: F] over the interval [MATH: [a,x].]

Content:
Let's see how to apply this formula to real-world problems.

items.title: Applications of Accumulation Functions

sections.normalized_html: Suppose that a pool has a small hole and that water is leaking out at a rate of [MATH: t^{1/3}] gallons per minute, where [MATH: t] is the time in minutes. If at time [MATH: t = 0] the pool contains [MATH: 100] gallons of water, how many gallons of water will remain in the pool after [MATH: t] minutes?
sections.readable_text: Suppose that a pool has a small hole and that water is leaking out at a rate of [MATH: t^{1/3}] gallons per minute, where [MATH: t] is the time in minutes. If at time [MATH: t = 0] the pool contains [MATH: 100] gallons of water, how many gallons of water will remain in the pool after [MATH: t] minutes?

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
Let [MATH: f(t) = -t^{1/3}] be the rate at which the volume of water in the pool is changing, and let [MATH: F(T)] be the amount of water in the pool after [MATH: T] minutes. Note that [MATH: f(t)] is negative to indicate that the volume is decreasing.

Using our formula for the accumulation of change, we have [MATH: F(T) = F(0) + \int_0^T f(t)\,\textrm d t.]

Substituting the known information and carrying out the necessary integration gives

[MATH: F(T)|= F(0) + ∫_{0}^{T}f(t)dt; = 100 − ∫_{0}^{T}t^{1/3}dt; = 100 − (3t^{4/3})/(4)|_{0}^{T}; = 100 − (3(T)^{4/3})/(4) + (3(0)^{4/3})/(4); = 100 − (3)/(4)T^{4/3}.]

Finally, let's rewrite our final answer in terms of the original variable [MATH: t.] We have

[MATH: F(t) = 100 - \dfrac {3}{4}t^{4/3}.]

Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
We're used to seeing definite integrals where the limits of integration are constants. For example,

Content:
[MATH: \displaystyle \int_{\color{red}0}^{\color{blue}{2}} t^2\,\textrm d t.]

Content:
Here, the lower limit is [MATH: t={\color{red}{0}}] and the upper limit is [MATH: t={\color{blue}{2}}.]

Content:
What do we get if we allow one of the integration limits to vary? Let's explore this idea by changing the upper integration limit to [MATH: t={\color{blue}{x}}.]

Content:
[MATH: \displaystyle \int_{\color{red}{0}}^{\color{blue}{x}} t^2\,\textrm d t]

Content:
We can evaluate this integral in the usual way:

Content:
[MATH: ∫_{0}^{x}t^{2}dt|= (1)/(3)t^{3}|_{0}^{x}; = (1)/(3)x^{3} − 0; = (1)/(3)x^{3}]

Content:
So, evaluating the integral now gives a function of [MATH: x] instead of a number. This means we can define a new function [MATH: F(x)] as

Content:
[MATH: F(x) = \int_0^x t^2\,\textrm d t.]

Content:
The function [MATH: F(x)] represents the area accumulated by the function [MATH: f(t)=t^2] between [MATH: t=0] and [MATH: t=x.] Different values of [MATH: x] will give different values for the area.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/812c461c1b7ac3a89eafaef2849bb2ce]

Content:
Any function [MATH: F(x)] defined as
[MATH: F(x) = \int_a^x f(t)\,\textrm d t]
is called an accumulation function.

---

Item 2 — Example: Evaluating an Accumulation Function

Example Prompt:
Calculate [MATH: F(\pi)] where [MATH: \displaystyle F(x) = \int_1^x \dfrac 1 t\,\textrm d t.]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
Evaluating [MATH: F(x)] at [MATH: x=\pi,] we get the following definite integral:
[MATH: F\!\left(\pi\right) = \int_{1}^{\pi} \dfrac{1}{t} \, \textrm{d}t]

Then, computing the definite integral, we get
[MATH: F(π)|= ∫_{1}^{π}(1)/(t)dt; = \ln|t||_{1}^{π}; = \ln π − \ln 1; = \ln π.]

Item 5 — Example: Evaluating an Accumulation Function Given a Graph

Example Prompt:
The graph of a function [MATH: y = f(x)] is shown below. Given [MATH: \displaystyle g(t)= \int_{-2}^{t} f(x)\, \textrm{d}x,] determine the value of [MATH: g(3).]

[IMG: /graphics/6a389b5bb31f7ee2ea2b8194d93fdc6d]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
Evaluating [MATH: g(t)] at [MATH: t=3,] we get the following definite integral:
[MATH: g(3) = \int_{-2}^{3} f(x)\, \textrm{d}x]

This integral gives the signed area between the curve and the [MATH: x]-axis shown below.

[IMG: /graphics/0c342ebdf2da41b0cc85cdb1342abbcd]

Note that the graph above consists of [MATH: 2] parts:

- [MATH: x \in [-2,0],] for which the region between the curve and the [MATH: x]-axis is a trapezoid. This corresponds to the area [MATH: A_1.]
- [MATH: x \in [0,3],] for which the region between the curve and the [MATH: x]-axis is another trapezoid. This corresponds to the area [MATH: A_2.]

Therefore, we can write the integral as follows:
[MATH: g(3) = \int_{-2}^{3} f(x) \, \textrm{d}x = \underbrace{\int_{-2}^{0} f(x) \, \textrm{d}x}_{A_1} + \underbrace{\int_{0}^{3} f(x) \, \textrm{d}x}_{A_2}]

Now, let's compute these integrals:

- To find the first integral where [MATH: x \in [-2,0],] we compute the area [MATH: A_1] of the trapezoid as follows:
[MATH: A_{1}|= (1)/(2) ⋅ 2 ⋅ (2 + 3); = 5]
- To find the second integral where [MATH: x \in [0,3],] we compute the area [MATH: A_2] of the trapezoid as follows:
[MATH: A_{2}|= (1)/(2) ⋅ 3 ⋅ (2 + 4); = 9]

Therefore, we obtain
[MATH: g(3)|= ∫_{− 2}^{3}f(x)dx = A_{1} + A_{2} = 5 + 9 = 14.]

Item 8 — Tutorial: The Accumulation Function of a Rate of Change

Content:
When we create an accumulation function by integrating a "rate of change" function, the accumulation function describes the "net change" of the system.

Content:
To describe this in more detail, suppose that [MATH: f(t)] is continuous and [MATH: F'(t) = f(t)] for [MATH: t\in [a,b].] From the fundamental theorem of calculus, we know that

Content:
[MATH: F(b) - F(a) = \int_a^b f(t)\,\textrm d t.]

Content:
The equation above can be rewritten as

Content:
[MATH: F(b) = F(a) + \int_a^b f(t)\,\textrm d t.]

Content:
If we let the upper limit vary, so setting [MATH: b=x,] we have

Content:
[MATH: F(x) = F(a) + \int_a^x f(t)\,\textrm d t.]

Content:
This formula tells us that the value of [MATH: F] at an arbitrary point [MATH: x] equals the value of [MATH: F] at some starting point [MATH: a] plus the accumulation of the rate of change of [MATH: F] over the interval [MATH: [a,x].]

Content:
Let's see how to apply this formula to real-world problems.

---

Item 9 — Example: Applications of Accumulation Functions

Example Prompt:
Suppose that a pool has a small hole and that water is leaking out at a rate of [MATH: t^{1/3}] gallons per minute, where [MATH: t] is the time in minutes. If at time [MATH: t = 0] the pool contains [MATH: 100] gallons of water, how many gallons of water will remain in the pool after [MATH: t] minutes?

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
Let [MATH: f(t) = -t^{1/3}] be the rate at which the volume of water in the pool is changing, and let [MATH: F(T)] be the amount of water in the pool after [MATH: T] minutes. Note that [MATH: f(t)] is negative to indicate that the volume is decreasing.

Using our formula for the accumulation of change, we have
[MATH: F(T) = F(0) + \int_0^T f(t)\,\textrm d t.]

Substituting the known information and carrying out the necessary integration gives

[MATH: F(T)|= F(0) + ∫_{0}^{T}f(t)dt; = 100 − ∫_{0}^{T}t^{1/3}dt; = 100 − (3t^{4/3})/(4)|_{0}^{T}; = 100 − (3(T)^{4/3})/(4) + (3(0)^{4/3})/(4); = 100 − (3)/(4)T^{4/3}.]

Finally, let's rewrite our final answer in terms of the original variable [MATH: t.] We have

[MATH: F(t) = 100 - \dfrac {3}{4}t^{4/3}.]
